name: Boost.Log
baseline: std::fstream with std::flush after every line (also stdio fprintf+fflush and g3log 1.3.2)
workload: Third-party logging benchmark by the author of the reckless logger: per-call latency for periodic calls, call bursts and calls interleaved with heavy disk I/O, plus total overhead of logging about one million lines from a multithreaded Mandelbrot computation, all with a synchronous Boost.Log text file sink writing to log.txt.
claimed_speedup: Mixed. Wins against std::fstream in two scenarios: 8-thread Mandelbrot overhead 1.82 vs 4.62 relative to reckless (about 2.5x lower, derived from page data) and the disk-I/O scenario 46.03 vs 5719.93 relative call latency (about 124x lower, derived from page data; fstream suffers multi-second synchronous flush stalls). Also beats g3log in periodic calls (67.42 vs 78.19) and call bursts (3.84 vs 4.20), and beats stdio (3.70) and g3log (3.09) in the 8-thread Mandelbrot overhead. Loses to spdlog, stdio and fstream in periodic calls and call bursts, and to everything but g3log in 1-thread Mandelbrot.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 and Boost 1.65.0 per the page; the optimisation flags of the published run are not stated (the benchmark build rules use -O3 when CONFIG_DEBUG is not 'yes', while tup.config.template defaults to CONFIG_DEBUG=yes).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X 3.7 GHz, 8 cores, SMT off; Samsung 970 EVO 1TB NVMe SSD; WD Red 3TB HDD on a Synology DS216j for the disk-I/O scenario; 32 GiB RAM; Linux 4.14.65
stars_or_usage: 212 stars; part of the Boost C++ Libraries
tradeoffs: Large, highly modular and extensible library (sources, filters, formatters, many sink backends) with a heavy abstraction level and Boost dependencies. The library's own README and docs (rationale, intro) state performance as a goal but publish no numbers; repo test/performance holds only internal timing programs (record_emission.cpp, dump.cpp) with no external baseline.
caveats: Boost.Log is not claimed to be fast by its authors, and the numbers come from a competitor's benchmark (reckless) in which Boost.Log is slower than reckless, spdlog and often plain stdio. Its wins are against std::fstream (disk-I/O scenario and 8-thread Mandelbrot) and g3log. The reckless adapter (benchmarks/boost_log.hpp) uses add_file_log without keywords::auto_flush, so Boost.Log does not flush after each record while the fstream and stdio adapters flush every line; this tilts the fstream comparison, and the 124x disk-I/O ratio is driven by multi-second synchronous flush stalls in fstream. Results are from Boost 1.65.0 and gcc 7.3.0 (the page predates current Boost releases), flags of the published run are not stated, and the page gives charts plus relative-time tables with IQR only. Other third-party shootouts show Boost.Log slower than the incumbents they list: NanoLog README latency table (Boost 1.55 1764 ns vs glog 1198 ns vs spdlog 214 ns, static string, 50th percentile) and an older spdlog README table (boost log 1.54 4.169 s vs glog 1.066 s vs spdlog 0.302 s for 1M lines, single thread; snippet only, page not opened, row no longer in the current README). Boost.org documentation was not reachable from this environment.

name: concurrencpp
baseline: libcoro thread_pool (jbaldwin/libcoro), with HPX as a second weaker baseline
workload: tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks recursive fork-join suite on 64 threads: skynet (100M tasks), nqueens, fib(39) and matmul(2048), measuring total wall time per runtime (peak RSS also reported).
claimed_speedup: Faster than libcoro on every fork-join benchmark: skynet 12514888 us vs 119686148 us (about 9.6x, derived from page data), nqueens 8000700 us vs 33347402 us (about 4.2x), fib(39) 20663744 us vs 238019884 us (about 11.5x), matmul(2048) 57383 us vs 374412 us (about 6.5x). Against HPX only matmul is faster (57383 us vs 59066 us, about 1.03x, within noise). Memory (separate cpp_tasks_bench repo, i7-8550U under WSL): 605972 kb vs Asio 853144 kb for 1M tasks (about 1.4x less, derived from page data).
hardware: EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13 Server, CPU boost enabled with schedutil governor
tradeoffs: C++20 coroutine task, executor, timer and result-object framework (thread pool, worker threads, manual and inline executors); full-featured API rather than a minimal work-stealing scheduler.
caveats: The project makes no numeric performance claim; the README only calls the design fast and clean, and the repo has no benchmark directory. The numbers come from a third-party suite written by the author of a competing runtime (TooManyCooks). In that same suite concurrencpp is far slower than the fast runtimes: mean ratio to best 258.19x (TBB 3.25x, taskflow 3.34x, cppcoro 3.67x, libfork 1.18x), for example skynet 12514888 us vs TBB 142887 us (about 88x slower, derived) and fib(39) 20663744 us vs TBB 215592 us (about 96x slower). The win over libcoro is against the slowest runtime in the table (mean ratio 2513.96x). Version of concurrencpp used by the suite is not stated on the README. Last commit is 'Version 0.1.7' dated 2023-07-15, over three years old. Memory results in cpp_tasks_bench lose to tokio (605972 kb vs 214136 kb for 1M tasks) and that repo states no compiler flags beyond a default Release build.
